Two keys sounding at once, as in Stravinsky’s Petrushka chord of C major against F♯ major.
A note held over from one chord into the next, where it clashes, then steps down to resolve.
A dissonant “leaning” note that arrives on a strong beat, unprepared, and moves by step to a chord note.
Borrowing notes or chords from the parallel minor or major, so that a tonic keeps its note but changes its colour.
A bass descending by step from the tonic to the dominant, a pattern that has signalled grief since the early seventeenth century.
Music made by combining independent melodic lines that fit together, as in fugue and canon.
One voice repeating another’s melody a moment later, at the same pitch or a different one.
Strict imitation: a melody followed note for note by other voices entering at a fixed distance; a round is a canon that can repeat endlessly.
A texture in which one line leads and the others support it, often moving in the same rhythm as chords.
Italian “obstinate”: a short phrase, rhythm or bass pattern repeated persistently while other things change above it.
A short musical idea — a few notes with a recognisable rhythm or contour — that a composer repeats and transforms.
A theme tied to a person, object or idea in a music drama, returning with changed harmony or orchestration as the story develops.
A work in several movements that brings back the same theme or themes in more than one of them.
The choice of which instruments play each line; it can change a melody’s colour and weight without changing a note.
Italian “divided”: a string section splits so that its players play different parts instead of the same one.
Plucking a string with the finger instead of drawing the bow across it, giving a short, dry note.
